nodes.label: Skipper a day trip
nodes.description: Take friends out for a full day and bring everyone home dry.

nodes.label: Leave the dock
nodes.description: Cast off and motor clear of the pontoon with someone who knows the harbour.

nodes.label: Tie a bowline
nodes.description: Practise it with your eyes closed, around a post and around your own waist, then untie it after it has held a load. A bowline makes a loop that will not slip or jam.

nodes.label: Sail with an instructor
nodes.description: Book a weekend course and spend both days at the tiller.

nodes.label: Read the weather
nodes.description: Check the forecast, the tide table and the sky before every sail, and write down what you expect.

nodes.label: Rig the boat alone
nodes.description: Step the mast, bend on the sails and run every line without help.

nodes.label: Tack and gybe
nodes.description: Turn through the wind and away from it until neither surprises you.

nodes.label: Capsize drill
nodes.description: Tip the boat over on purpose in warm water and right it.

nodes.label: First solo sail
nodes.description: An hour on the water with nobody else aboard.

nodes.label: Reef the main
nodes.description: Shorten sail at the mooring, then under way in a building breeze.

nodes.label: Heave to
nodes.description: Stop the boat in open water and let it sit quietly while you rest.

nodes.label: Sail at night
nodes.description: A short sail after dark, lights on and a torch on the compass.

nodes.label: Read a chart
nodes.description: Find the hazards, the buoys and the depths on the chart of your home waters.

nodes.label: Plan a coastal passage
nodes.description: Pick two harbours a day apart and plan the passage between them: the tides at each end, the hazards on the way, where to shelter if the wind rises, and the time you must leave to carry the tide. Write it on one page and show it to someone who has sailed it.

nodes.label: Learn the radio
nodes.description: Get the short-range radio licence and call the harbour once.

nodes.description: Cast off and motor clear of the pontoon with someone who knows the harbour.

nodes.label: Tie a bowline
nodes.description: Practise it with your eyes closed, around a post and around your own waist, then untie it after it has held a load. A bowline makes a loop that will not slip or jam.

nodes.label: Sail with an instructor
nodes.description: Book a weekend course and spend both days at the tiller.

nodes.label: Read the weather
nodes.description: Check the forecast, the tide table and the sky before every sail, and write down what you expect.

nodes.label: Rig the boat alone
nodes.description: Step the mast, bend on the sails and run every line without help.

nodes.label: Tack and gybe
nodes.description: Turn through the wind and away from it until neither surprises you.

nodes.label: Capsize drill
nodes.description: Tip the boat over on purpose in warm water and right it.

nodes.label: First solo sail
nodes.description: An hour on the water with nobody else aboard.

nodes.label: Reef the main
nodes.description: Shorten sail at the mooring, then under way in a building breeze.

nodes.label: Heave to
nodes.description: Stop the boat in open water and let it sit quietly while you rest.

nodes.label: Sail at night
nodes.description: A short sail after dark, lights on and a torch on the compass.

nodes.label: Read a chart
nodes.description: Find the hazards, the buoys and the depths on the chart of your home waters.

nodes.label: Plan a coastal passage
nodes.description: Pick two harbours a day apart and plan the passage between them: the tides at each end, the hazards on the way, where to shelter if the wind rises, and the time you must leave to carry the tide. Write it on one page and show it to someone who has sailed it.
